figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: PadLoc method overview on real data (tiles: intermediates of one trajectory chunk). A known floor plan, depth profiles, and planar odometry enter (1); the training-free back-end fuses a short window into a target and observation mask, which bounds drift (2), reduces rotation to four wall-angle heading candidates (3), scores translations with masked NCC and keeps top-$K$ peaks (4), propagates $K{\leq}10$ gated Gaussian hypotheses with odometry (5), and re-reads the raw NCC fields by consensus to choose the global anchor and recover poses (6; dashed: ground truth).
figures.headline: The pipeline reduces rotation to four wall-angle headings, then recovers poses by consensus from raw correlation fields.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Sliding-window matching and consensus decoding (cons). Columns show one trajectory from early ambiguity to the final anchor. Rows show the accumulated target, masked-NCC top-$K$ votes, GM-BF hypotheses, and the cumulative consensus readout.
figures.headline: On one trajectory, early ambiguity resolves into a single consensus anchor as windows accumulate.
citing_sentences: 2), split by what each can trust: the GM-BF combines each window’s top-$K$ peaks with odometry to place the windows relative to each other, correcting drift, and the consensus sum adds the aligned raw fields to fix one absolute anchor.

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Matcher cost vs. floor-plan size ($10\text{\,}\mathrm{cm}$ grid; RTX 3090). One UnLoc call scores all 36 orientations per frame; a PadLoc window scores all $B{\approx}4$ headings (solid; one heading dashed); complete back-end cost is given in the text. UnLoc grows →209 ms; a PadLoc window grows →13.7 ms ($15\times$ at mall scale, $76\times$ per frame at stride $5$; UnLoc is cheaper at home scale).
figures.headline: At mall scale, one PadLoc window costs 13.7 ms against 209 ms for one UnLoc call.
citing_sentences: With depth fixed, UnLoc scans the full DeSDF every frame over $O{=}36$ orientations and $V{=}11$ rays ($\mathcal{O}(HWOV)$), while PadLoc correlates one fused target over $B{\approx}4$ headings per $S{=}5$-frame window with cached reference FFTs ($\mathcal{O}(N\log N)$)—the Fig. 3 gap.

figures.label: Figure S1
figures.caption: Observation semantics on the blurred reference. (a) $\sigma$-blurred reference field. (b) A window target overlaid: yellow wall hits register on the blue reference bands, teal cells are observed free space, and unobserved cells drop out of the masked NCC.
figures.headline: Wall hits register on the blurred reference bands, while unobserved cells drop out of the masked statistic.
citing_sentences: Figure S1 details the observation raster sketched in the main paper’s teaser: wall hits carry mask weight $w_{\mathrm{wall}}$, traversed cells become observed free space whose zeros penalize overlapping reference walls, and unobserved cells drop out of the masked statistics entirely.

figures.label: Figure S2
figures.caption: Orientation pre-pass mechanism. Hough wall segments from the reference and accumulated target scan are converted into length-weighted wall-angle histograms. Cross-correlation aligns the target histogram to the reference axes and yields the directed heading set plus $180^{\circ}$ mirrors (here $4.0^{\circ}/94.2^{\circ}$), which masked NCC scores downstream.
figures.headline: Wall-angle histograms align target and reference, giving headings of 4.0° and 94.2° in this example.

figures.label: Figure S3
figures.caption: Cumulative top-$K$ NMS recall of the GT pose on the headline consensus decoder’s surface (moving-pose GM-BF $+$ consensus-sum, chunk-end readout, GT depth, $10\text{\,}\mathrm{cm}$ grid, $37$ gibson_t chunks; GT-hit and NMS separation $0.30\text{\,}\mathrm{m}$, quantization-fair at $10\text{\,}\mathrm{cm}$). $\sigma$ is per-frame odometry noise: a seeded random walk of $\sigma\,$cm on each translation axis and $\sigma^{\circ}$ on heading per frame. At $\sigma{=}2.0$ the global argmax recovers GT in only $62.2\text{\,}\mathrm{\%}$ of chunks, while the deployed $K{=}10$ (dashed) recovers $83.8\text{\,}\mathrm{\%}$ (top-$20$: $86.5\text{\,}\mathrm{\%}$); for $\sigma{\leq}0.5$ the argmax misses at most one chunk (at $\sigma{=}0$ one chunk is missed at every $K$).
figures.headline: At motion noise 2.0, the consensus argmax recovers the true pose in 62.2% of chunks, against 83.8% for top-10 peaks.
citing_sentences: Figure S3 examines residual multimodality under increasing motion noise: the global argmax of the consensus surface slips off ground truth on a growing fraction of chunks, while the true pose remains among its top-$K$ NMS peaks more often.

figures.label: Figure S4
figures.caption: Readout timing on Gibson ($T{=}15$, $W{=}S{=}5$, 1-based frames). Bars: windows; dot: pose stamp (end $-2$); triangle: output available after the window’s last frame; dashed line: first output. Grey band: the ten scored frames. Forward filters (F3Loc, UnLoc-fwd) emit one pose per frame. PadLoc frozen: each scored frame is coloured by the window that serves it, the latest window ended at or before that frame; numbers give the anchor age in frames. PadLoc delayed: all ten frames use the chunk-end anchor read at frame $T$.
figures.headline: Frozen readout serves each scored frame from the latest window that had ended, while delayed readout uses one chunk-end anchor.

figures.label: Figure S5
figures.caption: Hilti online pose error ($W/S{=}30/30$, with-windows reference). Per-frame error $\|\hat{x}-x_{\mathrm{gt}}\|$ vs. trajectory fraction for the five GT sessions; the legend lists frame count and mean error. Blue: localizing sessions; red: run_1 and UG1; dashed: $2\text{\,}\mathrm{m}$ threshold.
figures.headline: Hilti sessions that localize mostly stay under 2 m error, while the two failing sessions mostly exceed it.
citing_sentences: Figure S5 plots the per-frame localization error $\|\hat{x}-x_{\mathrm{gt}}\|$ of the online pose stream against trajectory fraction for all five Hilti GT sessions at the adopted $W/S{=}30/30$ (every GT frame, $T{=}2569$–$6124$ per session—the same per-frame statistic as the mean column of the main paper’s Table 5).

figures.label: Figure S6
figures.caption: Whole-run trajectory on floor_1. The online per-window estimate (purple) vs. ground truth (green) on the occupancy floor plan; the estimate tracks the full building loop (SR@$2\text{\,}\mathrm{m}$ $0.98$, median $0.81\text{\,}\mathrm{m}$).
figures.headline: On the first Hilti floor, the online estimate follows the full building loop, with 0.98 success at 2 m.
citing_sentences: Figure S6 shows the whole-run trajectory on floor_1, which tracks the full building loop.

figures.label: Figure S7
figures.caption: Per-window locking on floor_1 (qualitative). Nine of the 24 windows of the first 720 frames. Each panel shows the masked-NCC field (inferno), the depth target at the ground-truth pose (purple), the raw NCC peak (gold star), the decoded estimate (cyan ring), and GT (green plus).
figures.headline: Nine of 24 windows of one session show the raw correlation peak next to the decoded estimate and ground truth.
citing_sentences: Figure S7 shows a separate run over the first $720$ frames of the same session: nine of its $24$ non-overlapping $30$-frame windows, each cropped around the camera, with the per-window error in the panel title.

figures.label: Figure S8
figures.caption: Hilti failure taxonomy — three regimes. One row per regime. Columns: the two rectified camera views; the wall extraction placed on the plan at the ground-truth (red) and emitted (blue) pose, for a success and a failure window; and the per-window online error ($\pm 55^{\circ}$ multi-crop variant; dashed: $2\text{\,}\mathrm{m}$ success threshold). floor_1 fails by a parallel offset of a correct alignment; run_1’s off-plan walls localize on free space and fail by aliasing; UG1 reconstructs blobs, and its timeline also shows the recovery with learned wall segmentation ($+$seg, blue).
figures.headline: Hilti failures fall into three regimes: a parallel offset, aliasing on free space, and blob reconstructions.
citing_sentences: S8), separates the five sessions into three regimes, one per physical floor.
Its failures are aliasing: in $41$–$100\%$ of failed windows a wrong location explains the plan at least as well as the true pose (window 58 in Fig. S8).

figures.label: Figure S9
figures.caption: Per-call masked-NCC latency (RTX 3090, cuFFT) vs. target-window side on the $30\times 24$ m floor. Solid lines reuse the precomputed reference FFT; dashed lines rebuild it each call.
figures.headline: Reusing a precomputed reference transform is compared with rebuilding it each call on a real 30 by 24 m floor.
citing_sentences: Figure S9 sweeps the masked-NCC per-call latency on the RTX 3090 across matching cell and target-window size, on a real $30\times 24$ m benchmark floor (the synthetic up-scaled plans of §P reach mall scale).

figures.label: Figure S10
figures.caption: On-device power-of-two staircase (iPhone 15 Pro & 17 Pro, vDSP, $10\text{\,}\mathrm{cm}$, minimum over repeated calls). (a) Fixed $11\text{\,}\mathrm{m}$ target, growing floor plan; (b) fixed home plan, growing target. Both phones step through the same power-of-two FFT sizes and are flat within each size; the 17 Pro is ${\sim}1.2\times$ faster.
figures.headline: Latency stays flat within each power-of-two size on both iPhones, and the 17 Pro is 1.2× faster.
citing_sentences: We ran the same masked-NCC kernel on an iPhone 15 Pro and an iPhone 17 Pro (Accelerate/vDSP; Fig. S10, minimum over repeated calls).

abstract: We propose PadLoc, a training-free localization back-end that places a moving sensor within a known floor plan. Floor plans are cheap, persistent, and robust to appearance change, but recent learned-depth methods localize against them by filtering per-frame depth through dense $(x,y,\theta)$ pose grids. PadLoc keeps the swappable depth front-end and replaces the dense grid back-end with sparse geometric matching: dominant wall orientations define a small pose-candidate set, masked normalized cross-correlation scores observed free space against the plan, and a moving-pose Gaussian-mixture Bayes filter plus consensus readout decodes the trajectory. Holding each competitor’s depth fixed, PadLoc matches or beats UnLoc’s forward filter and the F3Loc filter at every Gibson trajectory length, and UnLoc’s offline refinement from $T{=}35$ on; it exceeds Z-FLoc’s published results with a shared MapAnything front-end. On Bonn LiLocBench, PadLoc improves pooled SR@1 m over UnLoc by $23$–$32$ pp under wheel odometry and $35$–$43$ pp with ground-truth motion; with full-FOV LiDAR plus wheel odometry the same readout reaches $100\text{\,}\mathrm{\%}$ SR@1 m at $9\text{\,}\mathrm{cm}10\text{\,}\mathrm{cm}$ median error on the static sequence. On the Hilti-Trimble Localization Challenge PadLoc localizes a camera-only fisheye rig on construction floors hundreds of metres across at $0.90$–$0.98$ online SR@2 m on three of five sessions; adding learned wall isolation, applied to every session, covers all five at $0.67$–$0.92$ with the localizer unchanged throughout. PadLoc thus matches or outperforms dense grid back-ends while preserving sensor modularity and a compact state that does not grow with trajectory length.

sections.body: The paper proposes PadLoc, a training-free localization back-end that places a moving sensor in a known floor plan. It keeps a swappable depth front-end and replaces the dense pose grid with a small set of dominant wall-orientation headings, masked normalized cross-correlation over translations, and a Gaussian-mixture Bayes filter with consensus readout. Holding each competitor's depth fixed, the authors report that PadLoc matches or beats UnLoc's forward filter and the F3Loc filter at every Gibson trajectory length. They also report transfer to Bonn and Hilti, and a state that does not grow with trajectory length.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: PadLoc replaces the dense pose grid in floor-plan localization with sparse geometric matching while keeping the depth front-end swappable.

sections.body: The section names F3Loc and UnLoc as the closest learned-depth baselines on Gibson. Both pair per-column depth with a dense recursive Bayes filter over x, y and heading, whereas PadLoc keeps a sparse translation posterior and uses dominant wall-orientation candidates. The matcher is placed among correlative scan matching methods and among Monte Carlo and Gaussian-sum trackers. Its masked correlation builds on Padfield's Fourier-domain formulation, and the stated contribution is exposing the full translation response as a multi-hypothesis posterior. Z-FLoc is compared only in the batched regime.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Related work positions PadLoc against dense grid filters and classical correlative and multi-hypothesis localization.

sections.body: The method rasterizes the floor plan once and builds, for each sliding window and candidate heading, a target raster with a validity mask. Observed free space penalizes overlapping reference walls, while unobserved cells drop out of the statistic. The masked correlation field is computed by Fourier-domain correlation, and its top local maxima form a sparse observation. A moving-pose Gaussian-mixture Bayes filter, capped at 10 components, combines these with odometry. A consensus readout sums the centred raw fields after alignment and emits poses at a bounded lag. Fixed constants were set on Gibson and not re-tuned.
sections.heading: Method
sections.headline: Masked normalized cross-correlation over a few wall-angle headings yields sparse peaks that a Gaussian-mixture filter and consensus sum decode into poses.

sections.body: The section compares back-ends with each depth source held fixed, over 9 Gibson scenes, scoring last-10-frame success at 1 m. With UnLoc's depth, PadLoc's frozen readout scores 0.731 at T=15, 0.840 at T=20, 0.919 at T=35, 1.000 at T=50 and 1.000 at T=100. UnLoc's forward filter scores 0.660, 0.710, 0.874, 0.923 and 0.973 at the same lengths. Under the chunk-end readout, UnLoc's forward filter equals its refinement in success at every length. The frozen readout exceeds the F3Loc filter by +5–24 pp on mono depth, and the batched matcher exceeds Z-FLoc's published results at every length. At T=15, a wrong wall family accounts for 37/72 failures on UnLoc depth.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: On Gibson, PadLoc's frozen readout beats UnLoc's forward filter at every trajectory length with matched depth.

sections.body: The limits section reports wrong-family heading ambiguity on very short sparse-depth trajectories, with 14–29% wrong-family chunks at T=15, because the free-space wedge is too small to reject the 180° mirror. Under high drift the filter can stay locked on a wrong basin, and the consensus peak-to-sidelobe ratio flags this without relocalizing. The method assumes stable wall structure, so furniture, renovations or long-term change make map quality decisive. On Hilti, the five sessions split into three regimes, and no variant is best on every session; no selector is evaluated. Fixed parameters were set on Gibson, and the Bonn lag sweeps concentrate on `static_0` at small n.
sections.heading: Discussion and Conclusion
sections.headline: The method still fails on very short sparse-depth trajectories, under high drift, and when floor-plan walls change.

sections.body: The appendix explains the observation raster and the blur applied to reference walls. It gives the numerical safeguards of the weighted masked correlation and reports how multiple hypotheses remain under increasing motion noise. A table of principal hyperparameters states how each value was set, and sensitivity sweeps cover the wall-hit weight, the depth-drop threshold and the fusion window. It also reports a negative result for weighting cells by depth confidence. Heading-error, per-scene and Hilti failure results, together with on-device latency measurements, follow.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: Appendix covers observation semantics, masked-correlation numerics, multi-hypothesis recall, hyperparameters, sensitivity sweeps, a depth-confidence ablation, and per-scene and failure tables.
